subtopic_detail: Spontaneous labour at thirty seven weeks after a previous classical uterine incision
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the birth suite for a thirty four year old woman in her second pregnancy who has arrived contracting strongly every four minutes at thirty seven weeks.

Her first baby was born at twenty seven weeks by caesarean section for severe early onset pre eclampsia, and the operation report from that admission records a vertical incision in the upper uterine segment. She had hoped for a vaginal birth this time and had not yet had her planned discussion about mode of birth. She is coping well with the contractions and the cardiotocograph is normal. The cervix is four centimetres dilated.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 94 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 140 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Contracting three in ten minutes lasting fifty seconds, cervix four centimetres dilated and eighty per cent effaced, membranes intact, vertex presenting at minus two station, abdomen not tender between contractions
data_table.Investigations: Cardiotocograph with normal baseline and variability and no decelerations, haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-155), group and hold sample sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Allow labour to continue with continuous cardiotocography and intravenous access, proceeding to caesarean only if the trace becomes abnormal or progress stalls
options.rationale: Continuous monitoring is the standard safeguard for a transverse lower segment scar, where rupture is rare and often heralded by fetal heart rate changes. With an upper segment scar, rupture can occur through the fundus without warning and before any trace abnormality. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

options.text: Offer epidural analgesia and review her progress in two hours, planning a caesarean section only if she has not reached full dilatation by that point
options.rationale: This defers an unavoidable operation while the uterus continues to contract against a scar that should not be laboured on, and epidural analgesia can mask the pain of a rupture. Every additional hour of labour adds risk without any prospect of safe vaginal birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

options.text: Give a tocolytic to abolish the contractions and arrange an elective caesarean section on the next available list after a full antenatal discussion
options.rationale: Tocolysis in established labour at four centimetres rarely succeeds and delays definitive management while the risk of rupture persists. The discussion she missed can be held while theatre is prepared. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

options.text: Arrange ultrasound measurement of the lower uterine segment thickness and use the result to decide between labour and immediate caesarean section
options.rationale: Segment thickness measurement is a research tool with no validated threshold for clinical decisions, and it assesses the lower segment while this scar lies in the fundus. It would delay the operation for information that cannot change it. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

options.text: Proceed to caesarean section now, informing the anaesthetic and theatre teams and counselling her about the reason while preparations are made
options.rationale: A vertical incision in the upper segment carries a rupture risk of several per cent in labour, many times that of a transverse lower segment scar, and rupture is often catastrophic and poorly predicted by monitoring. Labour is therefore not offered and birth proceeds before labour advances further. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

explanation.summary: Planned vaginal birth after caesarean is appropriate for most women with a single previous transverse lower segment incision, in whom the rupture risk is under one per cent and is usually signalled by fetal heart rate abnormality. A classical or other upper segment vertical incision is different in kind, with a reported rupture risk of several per cent, a tendency to rupture before labour begins and a presentation that is often sudden fetal collapse or maternal haemodynamic compromise rather than a gradual trace change. Such women are counselled antenatally for a planned caesarean at around thirty six to thirty seven weeks, and one who presents in labour needs the operation without delay. Very preterm caesarean sections, particularly before around twenty eight weeks when the lower segment is poorly formed, are the usual reason a classical incision was used, so the operation record from a previous very preterm birth must always be obtained rather than assumed. Other contraindications to planned vaginal birth include previous uterine rupture, previous transmural myomectomy and the usual obstetric indications for caesarean.
key_points: A classical or upper segment vertical scar contraindicates labour.
Rupture of such a scar may occur without warning and without preceding trace changes.
Previous very preterm caesarean is the usual reason a classical incision was used.
Always obtain the operation report rather than relying on the number of previous caesareans.
Planned birth is arranged at around thirty six to thirty seven weeks when the scar is classical.
explanation.pearls: Sudden constant abdominal pain between contractions, loss of the presenting station on vaginal examination and a fetal bradycardia are the classical triad of uterine rupture, and maternal tachycardia with shoulder tip pain from haemoperitoneum can appear before any vaginal bleeding is seen.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section
Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Vaginal birth after caesarean

subtopic_detail: Hepatitis B surface antigen positive at booking with a viral load above 200000 international units per millilitre
stem:
You are the doctor running the antenatal clinic reviewing a twenty five year old woman at fourteen weeks in her first pregnancy. She was born overseas and has known chronic hepatitis B infection acquired in childhood, and she has never needed treatment.

Her booking bloods confirm hepatitis B surface antigen and e antigen positivity with a viral load of 4 x 10^7 international units per millilitre. Liver enzymes are normal and an ultrasound of the liver shows no cirrhosis. She is not co infected with hepatitis C or human immunodeficiency virus. She asks what can be done to stop the baby catching the infection.

data_table.Examination: No jaundice, no stigmata of chronic liver disease, liver not enlarged, uterus consistent with dates, body mass index 22 kg/m2
data_table.Investigations: Hepatitis B surface antigen positive, e antigen positive, viral load 4 x 10^7 international units per millilitre, alanine aminotransferase 24 units per litre (5-35), platelets 246 x10^9/L (150-400), hepatitis C and human immunodeficiency virus serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management to reduce transmission?

options.text: Advise against breastfeeding to avoid postnatal transmission, and ensure the baby receives both immunoglobulin and vaccine within twelve hours of the birth
options.rationale: Breastfeeding is safe once the infant has received immunoprophylaxis and is actively encouraged, provided nipples are not cracked and bleeding. Discouraging it causes harm without reducing transmission. (Source: ASHM: Hepatitis B in pregnancy)

options.text: Start maternal pegylated interferon now to reduce the viral load before the birth, with neonatal immunoglobulin and vaccine given within twelve hours
options.rationale: Interferon is contraindicated in pregnancy because of antiproliferative effects on the fetus, and it is not used for this indication. The nucleotide analogue with the best pregnancy safety data is preferred. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Start maternal tenofovir in the third trimester and ensure the baby receives both immunoglobulin and vaccine within twelve hours of birth
options.rationale: Immunoprophylaxis alone fails in a meaningful proportion of babies born to women with very high viral loads, and third trimester antiviral therapy reduces that residual transmission. The combination of maternal suppression and timely neonatal immunoprophylaxis is what brings transmission close to zero. (Source: ASHM: Hepatitis B in pregnancy)

options.text: Rely on neonatal immunoglobulin and vaccine given within twelve hours of birth, and review her viral load again in the third trimester without treatment
options.rationale: Immunoprophylaxis is essential but leaves a failure rate of around five to ten per cent when the maternal viral load is this high. Measuring the load without acting on it wastes the opportunity to suppress it before birth. (Source: ASHM: Hepatitis B in pregnancy)

options.text: Plan an elective caesarean section at term and ensure the baby receives both immunoglobulin and vaccine within twelve hours of the birth
options.rationale: Mode of birth is not an established determinant of vertical transmission for this virus, unlike the situation with unsuppressed human immunodeficiency virus. Operative birth would add maternal morbidity without reducing infant risk. (Source: RANZCOG: Routine antenatal assessment)

explanation.summary: All pregnant women in Australia are screened for hepatitis B surface antigen at booking, and infants of positive women receive hepatitis B immunoglobulin plus the birth dose of vaccine within twelve hours, followed by the routine schedule and serological testing at around nine to twelve months. That combination prevents most vertical transmission, but it fails in roughly five to ten per cent of infants when the maternal viral load is very high, and e antigen positivity is a marker of that risk. Australian guidance therefore adds maternal antiviral therapy from around twenty eight to thirty two weeks when the viral load exceeds two hundred thousand international units per millilitre, using tenofovir disoproxil because it has the largest safety dataset in pregnancy and a high barrier to resistance. Therapy is usually continued for a period after the birth with monitoring of liver enzymes for a postpartum flare. Caesarean section confers no established benefit and breastfeeding is encouraged once the infant has been immunised.
key_points: Universal antenatal screening identifies women whose infants need immunoprophylaxis.
Immunoglobulin plus vaccine within twelve hours of birth is required for every exposed infant.
Maternal antiviral therapy is added when the viral load exceeds two hundred thousand international units per millilitre.
Tenofovir disoproxil is the preferred agent in pregnancy.
Breastfeeding is safe after immunoprophylaxis and caesarean birth does not reduce transmission.
explanation.pearls: Watch for a hepatitis flare in the months after birth, when immune reconstitution can raise transaminases sharply, particularly if antiviral therapy is stopped, so liver enzymes are checked at intervals through the first six postpartum months rather than assuming the risk ends at delivery.

subtopic_detail: Maternal fever with fetal tachycardia two days after membrane rupture at thirty weeks
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a thirty three year old woman admitted two days ago with ruptured membranes at thirty weeks. She completed a course of betamethasone and has been receiving oral antibiotics as part of expectant management.

Overnight she developed lower abdominal discomfort and now feels hot and shivery. The midwife reports that the liquor draining onto the pad has become offensive. She has no contractions. The cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 178 beats per minute with reduced variability and no decelerations, and the neonatal unit has a cot available.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 122 beats per minute, blood pressure 106/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in room air, temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 178 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Uterus tender on palpation between contractions, offensive liquor draining, cervix long and closed on speculum examination, no calf tenderness, chest clear on auscultation
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 22.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C reactive protein 148 mg/L (less than 5), lactate 2.4 mmol/L (0.5-2.2), urinalysis negative for nitrites and leucocytes, cardiotocograph with a baseline of 178 beats per minute and reduced variability

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give intravenous antibiotics with tocolysis and magnesium sulfate, arranging transfer to a quaternary centre with a higher level neonatal intensive care unit
options.rationale: Tocolysis is contraindicated in the presence of intrauterine infection because prolonging the pregnancy is the harm, and transfer is unnecessary when a suitable cot is already available on site. Magnesium for neuroprotection is reasonable but must not delay the birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm labour)

options.text: Start intravenous broad spectrum antibiotics and expedite the birth, involving the neonatal and anaesthetic teams while resuscitation continues
options.rationale: Intrauterine infection is the one situation in which expectant management after preterm rupture of membranes is abandoned, because the uterus is the source and both mother and fetus deteriorate while it remains in place. Antibiotics alone do not achieve source control. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.text: Change to intravenous broad spectrum antibiotics and continue expectant management, reassessing in six hours to see whether the fever has responded
options.rationale: Waiting for a fever to settle while the infected uterus remains undelivered exposes the fetus to worsening inflammation and the mother to septic shock. Fetal inflammatory injury accumulates during precisely this interval. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.text: Give intravenous antibiotics and a second course of corticosteroids, deferring the birth for twenty four hours so that the fetus gains the full benefit
options.rationale: A repeat steroid course has no place when infection mandates immediate birth, and delaying for it trades a marginal respiratory benefit for a substantial infective risk. The first course has already been completed. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal corticosteroids)

options.text: Perform amniocentesis to sample the liquor for glucose, Gram stain and culture, and decide on the timing of birth once those results are available
options.rationale: Amniotic fluid analysis is used when the diagnosis is genuinely uncertain, not when fever, uterine tenderness, offensive liquor, maternal tachycardia and fetal tachycardia are all present. The clinical diagnosis is already made and the delay would be dangerous. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

explanation.summary: Expectant management after preterm prelabour rupture of membranes aims to gain gestational maturity, and it is supported by corticosteroids, latency antibiotics and surveillance for infection. Chorioamnionitis ends that strategy immediately, because the infected uterine contents are the source and both fetal inflammatory response syndrome and maternal sepsis progress while the pregnancy continues. The diagnosis is clinical, supported by maternal fever, maternal and fetal tachycardia, uterine tenderness, offensive liquor and rising inflammatory markers, and no single test is required to confirm it. Management is intravenous broad spectrum antibiotics with prompt birth, by induction where labour can be achieved safely and by caesarean where it cannot, with neonatal and anaesthetic teams involved early. Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection may still be given at this gestation provided it does not delay the birth, and a repeat corticosteroid course is not a reason to wait.
key_points: Chorioamnionitis converts expectant management into expedited birth.
The diagnosis is clinical and does not require amniocentesis.
Antibiotics without source control do not stop fetal inflammatory injury.
Tocolysis is contraindicated once intrauterine infection is suspected.
Neuroprotective magnesium may be given provided it does not delay the birth.
explanation.pearls: Fetal tachycardia above one hundred and sixty beats per minute with reduced variability is often the first sign of intrauterine infection and can precede maternal fever, so a rising baseline in a woman managed expectantly after membrane rupture warrants reassessment for infection rather than simple observation.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

subtopic_detail: Positive syphilis serology at booking in a woman reporting anaphylaxis to penicillin
stem:
You are the doctor in the antenatal clinic reviewing a twenty two year old woman at sixteen weeks in her first pregnancy. Her booking serology is reactive for syphilis with a rapid plasma reagin titre of 1 in 32, and treponemal specific testing is positive.

She has never been treated and a repeat sample confirms the titre. She recalls facial swelling and difficulty breathing after amoxicillin as a teenager and has avoided penicillins since. She has no rash, no oral or genital ulcers and no neurological or ocular symptoms. The sexual health service can see her this week.

data_table.Examination: No rash on the trunk, palms or soles, no genital or oral ulceration, no lymphadenopathy, no cranial nerve abnormality, uterus consistent with dates
data_table.Investigations: Rapid plasma reagin titre 1 in 32 confirmed on a second sample, treponemal specific antibody positive, human immunodeficiency virus and hepatitis serology negative, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment plan?

options.text: Defer treatment until after the birth given the allergy history, and treat the newborn with a full course of parenteral penicillin under paediatric supervision
options.rationale: Untreated maternal infection causes stillbirth, hydrops, preterm birth and congenital disease long before term, so deferral is not an option. Treating the baby afterwards cannot reverse injury that occurred in utero. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines: Syphilis)

options.text: Admit her for penicillin desensitisation in a monitored setting and then treat with intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin according to the disease stage
options.rationale: Penicillin is the only agent reliably shown to treat the fetus as well as the mother, so a documented allergy is managed by desensitisation rather than by substitution. The procedure is performed where anaphylaxis can be treated immediately. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines: Syphilis)

options.text: Treat her with oral doxycycline for the appropriate duration for the stage of infection and repeat the serological titre monthly until the birth
options.rationale: Tetracyclines are contraindicated in pregnancy because of effects on fetal bone and teeth, and they do not cross the placenta in concentrations that treat congenital infection. Serological follow up cannot make up for inadequate fetal treatment. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines: Syphilis)

options.text: Treat her with a course of oral azithromycin and arrange serological follow up with monthly titres and detailed ultrasound assessment of the fetus
options.rationale: Macrolide resistance in this organism is widespread and treatment failures with fetal infection have been documented, so it is not an acceptable alternative in pregnancy. Ultrasound surveillance detects established fetal disease rather than preventing it. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines: Syphilis)

options.text: Treat her with a course of intravenous ceftriaxone in the day unit and arrange repeat serology at delivery to confirm an adequate response to the treatment
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone has activity but the evidence for preventing congenital infection is limited, and cross reactivity is a consideration in genuine penicillin anaphylaxis. It is not the recommended pathway when desensitisation is available. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Syphilis is rising in Australia, with outbreaks that have produced congenital cases, so all women are screened at booking and many jurisdictions now repeat testing in the third trimester and at birth in higher incidence regions. Benzathine benzylpenicillin is the only treatment proven to prevent congenital infection, because alternatives either fail to cross the placenta adequately or have documented treatment failures, and this makes desensitisation the standard response to a reported penicillin allergy in pregnancy. Desensitisation is performed in a monitored setting with escalating oral or intravenous doses over several hours and is followed immediately by treatment, since tolerance is lost within days of stopping. The number of weekly doses depends on the stage, with a single dose for early infection and three weekly doses for late or unknown duration disease, and missing a dose in pregnancy means restarting the course. A Jarisch Herxheimer reaction after the first dose can cause fever, uterine contractions and fetal heart rate changes, so treatment in the second half of pregnancy is given where fetal monitoring is available.
key_points: Penicillin is the only treatment that reliably treats the fetus.
Reported penicillin allergy in pregnancy is managed by desensitisation, not substitution.
Doxycycline is contraindicated and macrolide resistance makes azithromycin unreliable.
Staging determines whether one dose or three weekly doses are given.
Untreated infection causes stillbirth, hydrops, preterm birth and congenital disease.
explanation.pearls: Warn about the Jarisch Herxheimer reaction within hours of the first dose, since fever with uterine contractions and transient fetal heart rate abnormality is common in the second half of pregnancy and is regularly mistaken for chorioamnionitis or preterm labour, prompting unnecessary intervention.

subtopic_detail: Thromboprophylaxis duration after emergency caesarean in a woman with a body mass index of 39
stem:
You are the obstetric resident writing the discharge plan for a thirty six year old woman who had an emergency caesarean section at term for failure to progress after a long labour.

Her body mass index at booking was 39 kg/m2 and she is now thirty six hours post operative. She has been slow to mobilise because of pain and has needed a urinary catheter overnight. Her mother had a pulmonary embolism after a hip replacement. She is breastfeeding, has no wound concerns, and has been receiving enoxaparin since the evening after surgery. She asks how long she will need the injections at home.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 17 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Wound dry with no erythema, uterus well contracted, calves soft and non tender with no asymmetry, chest clear on auscultation, mobilising slowly with assistance
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-155), platelets 268 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 62 micromol/L (45-90), estimated blood loss at operation 700 mL

lead_in: What is the most appropriate thromboprophylaxis plan?

options.text: Change to oral rivaroxaban for six weeks after the birth, with graduated compression stockings and advice on early mobilisation while breastfeeding
options.rationale: Direct oral anticoagulants enter breast milk and lack safety data in lactation, so they are avoided while breastfeeding. Low molecular weight heparin is not secreted in clinically significant amounts and remains the drug of choice. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Stop the heparin now given her postoperative blood loss and falling haemoglobin, and rely on graduated compression stockings with early mobilisation
options.rationale: A blood loss of this order with a stable haemoglobin and a dry wound is not a contraindication to prophylactic dosing. Withholding prophylaxis in a high risk woman exchanges a small bleeding concern for a life threatening thrombotic one. (Source: RANZCOG: Thromboprophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Thromboprophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Continue low molecular weight heparin for six weeks after the birth, with graduated compression stockings and advice on early mobilisation
options.rationale: Emergency caesarean after prolonged labour, obesity, immobility and a first degree family history combine to place her in the highest postnatal risk category, for which extended prophylaxis to six weeks is recommended. Risk remains elevated across the whole puerperium rather than only the first week. (Source: RANZCOG: Thromboprophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Thromboprophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Continue low molecular weight heparin until discharge from hospital, then use graduated compression stockings alone with advice on early mobilisation
options.rationale: Stopping at discharge covers only a fraction of the period of raised risk, and most postnatal events occur after the woman has gone home. Stockings alone are inadequate for a woman with several persisting risk factors. (Source: RANZCOG: Thromboprophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Thromboprophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Continue low molecular weight heparin for ten days after the birth, with graduated compression stockings and advice on early mobilisation
options.rationale: A shorter course suits women whose only risk factor is the caesarean itself, whereas the accumulation of risk factors here moves her into the extended duration group. The distinction between the two durations is the point being tested. (Source: RANZCOG: Thromboprophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Thromboprophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

explanation.summary: Venous thromboembolism remains a leading direct cause of maternal death in Australia, and the risk is highest in the first week after birth but stays above baseline for about six weeks. Australian units use risk scoring that counts caesarean section, particularly emergency caesarean after labour, obesity, age, parity, immobility, prolonged labour, postpartum haemorrhage, pre eclampsia, infection, a family history in a first degree relative and known thrombophilia. Women with a single moderate risk factor generally receive prophylaxis for about ten days, while those with a combination of factors or a high risk feature receive it for six weeks after the birth. Low molecular weight heparin is the agent of choice because it does not cross into breast milk in clinically significant amounts, whereas direct oral anticoagulants are avoided in lactation. Prophylactic dosing is compatible with wound healing, and dose adjustment for weight is necessary in obesity.
key_points: Postnatal thrombotic risk remains elevated for about six weeks.
Risk factors are counted cumulatively rather than singly.
A single moderate factor usually warrants about ten days of prophylaxis.
Multiple factors or a high risk feature warrant six weeks.
Low molecular weight heparin is compatible with breastfeeding, unlike direct oral anticoagulants.
explanation.pearls: Prophylactic enoxaparin is dosed by weight rather than given as a fixed dose, because a woman over about ninety kilograms receiving the standard forty milligram dose is underdosed, and weight banded prescribing is a recurring gap identified in maternal mortality reviews.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Thromboprophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium
BMJ Best Practice: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Anticoagulation choice at six weeks for a mechanical mitral valve maintained on a low daily warfarin dose
stem:
You are the physician in a joint obstetric medicine clinic seeing a thirty one year old woman who has just discovered she is six weeks pregnant. She has a bileaflet mechanical mitral valve replacement performed eight years ago for rheumatic disease and takes warfarin 2.5 mg daily, with an international normalised ratio that has remained in range at every recent check.

She is in sinus rhythm with good ventricular function on her last echocardiogram and has never had a thromboembolic event. She has read online that her tablets cause birth defects and has already missed two doses out of concern. She wants whichever plan gives her the best chance of a healthy baby and of surviving the pregnancy herself.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Crisp mechanical first heart sound with no murmur of regurgitation, jugular venous pressure not raised, chest clear on auscultation, no peripheral oedema, no signs of embolic phenomena
data_table.Investigations: International normalised ratio 2.8 (target 2.5-3.5), haemoglobin 126 g/L (115-155), platelets 232 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 58 micromol/L (45-90), echocardiogram three months ago with normal prosthetic gradients and normal ventricular function

lead_in: What anticoagulation strategy should you recommend?

options.text: Continue warfarin through the first trimester after full counselling, and change to heparin in the weeks before the planned birth
options.rationale: Embryopathy risk is dose related and is low at daily doses at or below five milligrams, while warfarin gives the most reliable protection against valve thrombosis, which carries high maternal and fetal mortality. Substitution near term avoids an anticoagulated fetus during labour. (Source: RANZCOG: Cardiac disease in pregnancy)

options.text: Change to therapeutic low molecular weight heparin for the whole pregnancy, with anti factor Xa monitoring and dose adjustment at intervals
options.rationale: Heparin avoids embryopathy but carries a clearly higher rate of valve thrombosis, and failures cluster in women whose peak levels look adequate but whose trough levels fall. It is the preferred option when the warfarin dose required is high rather than low. (Source: RANZCOG: Cardiac disease in pregnancy)

options.text: Change to prophylactic low molecular weight heparin with low dose aspirin for the first trimester, then return to warfarin for the remainder
options.rationale: Prophylactic dosing is far below what a mechanical mitral prosthesis requires and aspirin does not substitute for anticoagulation. This combination would leave her substantially unprotected during the period of change. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Change to unfractionated heparin by continuous intravenous infusion for the first trimester in hospital, then restart warfarin in the second trimester
options.rationale: Continuous infusion achieves protection but commits a well woman to twelve weeks as an inpatient with line related infection and bleeding risks. It is reserved for the peripartum period or for women in whom other options have failed. (Source: RANZCOG: Cardiac disease in pregnancy)

options.text: Change to a direct oral anticoagulant for the pregnancy because it avoids both the embryopathy risk and the burden of frequent monitoring visits
options.rationale: Direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated with mechanical valves in any patient after trials showed excess thromboembolism and bleeding, and they are not used in pregnancy. This option is unsafe on two independent grounds. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: A mechanical valve in pregnancy sets maternal thrombotic risk against fetal teratogenic risk, and no strategy removes both. Warfarin provides the most reliable protection against valve thrombosis but crosses the placenta and causes an embryopathy of nasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses when taken between about six and twelve weeks, together with fetal intracranial haemorrhage later in pregnancy. Crucially the embryopathy risk is dose dependent, falling to around two to three per cent at daily doses of five milligrams or less, which is why international and Australian guidance supports continuing warfarin through the first trimester at low dose after explicit counselling, while recommending substitution of heparin when the required dose is higher. Low molecular weight heparin does not cross the placenta but carries a higher rate of valve thrombosis even with anti factor Xa monitoring, partly because trough levels fall between doses, and mitral prostheses are more thrombogenic than aortic ones. Warfarin is changed to heparin at around thirty six weeks so that the fetus is not anticoagulated during labour, and a woman who presents in labour on warfarin needs caesarean birth to avoid fetal intracranial haemorrhage.
key_points: Warfarin embryopathy risk is dose dependent and low at five milligrams daily or less.
Valve thrombosis carries high mortality for both mother and fetus.
Low molecular weight heparin avoids embryopathy but has a higher thrombosis rate.
Mitral prostheses are more thrombogenic than aortic prostheses.
Direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated with any mechanical valve.
explanation.pearls: If she presents in labour while still taking warfarin, the fetus is anticoagulated even when the maternal international normalised ratio has been reversed, so caesarean birth is chosen to avoid intracranial haemorrhage from the pressures of a vaginal birth, and vitamin K given to the mother does not protect the baby quickly enough.

sources.label: European Society of Cardiology: Cardiovascular disease during pregnancy
